analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers to cover people with preexisting conditions and spreads the cost of the sickest patients through a federal reinsurance fund.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors and heard once in subcommittee, the bill never got a committee or floor vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set national standards for employer health insurance: insurers would have to sell coverage to any employer that applies, renew it every year, cap deductibles and out-of-pocket costs, and base premiums on the average cost of covering everyone in a state rather than each group's health risks. It would also create a federal Health Reinsurance Trust Fund that pays plans back once any one person's core benefits top $25,000 in a year, financed by a per-person excise tax on all health plans. Insurers that refused to follow the standards would owe a tax equal to 100 percent of their health premiums.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees and their families in employer health plans, especially anyone with a preexisting condition, a chronic illness, or high out-of-pocket costs. Insurers could no longer refuse to cover a group, could not exclude a person's preexisting condition beyond the first six months, and could not cancel coverage for using benefits heavily. People leaving a job could convert to individual coverage at no more than 150 percent of the community rate without a health screening. Plans would be repaid for the costliest patients, so covering sick workers would no longer threaten any single plan's finances.

how_it_helps.text: Every insurer would have to sell coverage to any employer seeking it and renew the contract each year unless there was cause like nonpayment or fraud — not the group's health risks.

Insurers could not exclude an eligible employee, spouse, or dependent from coverage, and preexisting-condition exclusions could last no more than six months, with full coverage for high-risk individuals without price differences within a community or cancellation for heavy usage.

Premiums would be community-rated — set by the average cost of covering everyone a plan insures, rather than by each group's health history — so sick employees would not make one employer's premiums unaffordable.

Policies would have to offer a core benefit package modeled on Medicare, with deductibles capped at $500, out-of-pocket costs capped at $2,500 per year, and no cost-sharing for children's preventive care or pregnancy-related services.

A federal Health Reinsurance Trust Fund, financed by an excise tax on each health plan, would reimburse plans for core benefits above $25,000 per person per year, spreading the cost of the sickest patients across the whole market.
Workers leaving group coverage could convert to individual policies at no more than 150 percent of the community rate, with no waiting period and regardless of health.

Enforcement was blunt: an insurer that failed the standards would owe a tax equal to 100 percent of the gross premiums it collected on all its health policies for the year, with waivers only for unknowing or promptly corrected failures.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers bear the direct cost: a tax of 100 percent of gross premiums for failing the standards, plus a per-covered-person stop-loss excise tax on every plan that funds the reinsurance pool. Self-insured employer plans and HMOs also pay the per-person tax. Insurers would pass much of that through to employers and enrollees in premiums, and the bill preempts state rules requiring benefits richer than the core package.

drawbacks.text: The stop-loss excise tax applies to every covered person in every qualified plan — including self-insured employer plans and HMOs — raising the cost of providing coverage, which employers and enrollees would ultimately bear.

A penalty equal to 100 percent of an insurer's entire health premium revenue is so severe that small insurers might exit the market rather than risk it, and the bill itself includes waivers and a 30-day correction window, acknowledging the tax could be triggered by ordinary administrative mistakes.

The bill preempts state laws that require health contracts offering core benefits to cover additional services or provider types, so states could not mandate benefits richer than the federal core package on those contracts.

The reinsurance backstop cushions insurers from the high-cost patients the standards force them to cover, meaning part of the bill's consumer protection is paid for by a broad tax on all health plans rather than only by the insurers whose pricing practices created the problem.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections were substantial and the design showed awareness of the biggest risk: pairing guaranteed issue and community rating with a reinsurance pool so that covering sick people would not send premiums spiraling for everyone else. The costs were real but conventional — a tax on all plans to fund high-cost cases and a blunt penalty to force compliance. The genuine trade-offs are the preemption of state benefit mandates and the sheer severity of the 100-percent penalty, but on balance the bill traded insurer pricing freedom for guaranteed, standardized, portable coverage for people in employer plans.

outcome.mechanism: The bill got one hearing in a Ways and Means subcommittee, was never voted on in committee or on the House floor, and died when the two-year Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the Health Insurance Reform Act of 1991 on April 29, 1991, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee.
No one from either party signed on as a cosponsor — the bill had zero cosponsors for its entire life.
On May 6, 1991 it was sent to the Health Subcommittee, which held a hearing on March 12, 1992 — the only public action the bill ever received.
The committee never held a markup or voted to report the bill, the House never debated it, and it expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers were better off: the bill that would have forced guaranteed issue, community rating, and coverage of preexisting conditions never advanced, so risk-based underwriting stayed in place. The people the bill was written for — those denied coverage or priced out because of health history — gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers who avoided new rules

sides.party_line_note: No committee or floor votes were ever held, and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so there is no recorded partisan split — only a single Democratic sponsor [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have stripped insurers of risk-based pricing and coverage denials — guaranteed issue, guaranteed renewal, six-month cap on preexisting-condition exclusions, and community-rated premiums, enforced by a tax of 100 percent of premiums for noncompliance. But the same bill created a federal reinsurance fund that repays plans once a person's care tops $25,000 a year, cushioning the industry from exactly the high-cost patients the new rules force it to cover [S3, S2].

Employer plans would owe the new per-person stop-loss excise tax, but they would also qualify for reinsurance reimbursements above $25,000 per employee per year — a net shield against catastrophic claims for workers with serious illnesses [S3].

Qualified HMOs are excluded from the 100-percent penalty tax and would owe only the per-person stop-loss tax, while gaining access to the reinsurance fund if they cover at least the core benefits [S3].

industries.industry: State insurance regulators and benefit-mandate laws
industries.note: The bill preempts state laws requiring services or provider types beyond the federal core benefits on contracts offering only that core package, narrowing states' ability to require richer coverage [S3].
